config.title: z-index and stacking context

intro.title: z-index and stacking context
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage with overlapping colored boxes to visually explore how z-index controls the stacking order of elements. You will learn the core concept of stacking context, which determines how elements are layered on top of each other. The main technology involved is CSS, using properties like position and z-index. By the end, you'll understand how to use z-index effectively to manage which elements appear in front or behind others.
intro.usecase: The z-index property is essential for managing overlapping UI elements in real-world interfaces. Developers use it to control stacking order in complex layouts like navigation dropdowns that must appear above page content, modal dialogs that overlay everything, or tooltips that float above form fields. In dashboards with multiple panels, cards, and data visualizations, z-index ensures interactive elements like hover states or notification badges remain visible. Understanding stacking context prevents common bugs where elements unexpectedly appear behind others despite having higher z-index values.

steps.title: Create HTML structure with three overlapping boxes
steps.instruction: Create a simple HTML file with three div elements that will overlap each other. Use the class names 'box box1', 'box box2', and 'box box3' for the three divs.
steps.hint: Start with a basic HTML structure and add three div elements inside the body. Give each div a class attribute with 'box' and a unique second class (box1, box2, box3).
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>z-index Demo</title>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add three div elements with classes 'box box1', 'box box2', and 'box box3' here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a complete HTML file with three div elements ready for styling to demonstrate overlapping.
successCriteria: The HTML file contains three div elements with class attributes 'box box1', 'box box2', and 'box box3'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly three div elements with the correct class names: 'box box1', 'box box2', and 'box box3'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a simple HTML file with three div elements that will overlap. Each div should have a class attribute with 'box' and a unique identifier (box1, box2, box3).

steps.title: Apply z-index to control stacking order
steps.instruction: Add z-index values to the .box1, .box2, and .box3 CSS rules to control which box appears on top. Give each box a different z-index value.
steps.hint: Use the z-index property in your CSS. Higher values appear on top of lower values. Try giving box1 z-index: 1, box2 z-index: 2, and box3 z-index: 3.

Box 2
Box 3
steps.expectedOutcome: The boxes will have different z-index values applied, changing which box appears visually on top of the others.
successCriteria: All three box classes (.box1, .box2, .box3) have z-index properties with different numeric values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some z-index values, but make sure all three boxes (.box1, .box2, .box3) have z-index properties with different values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The z-index properties aren't properly applied. Check that you've added z-index values to all three box classes in the CSS.

steps.hint: Set opacity to a decimal between 0 and 1, for example: opacity: 0.7;

steps.expectedOutcome: Box 1 will have its own stacking context due to opacity being less than 1, which may affect how z-index values are interpreted relative to other boxes.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added opacity, but make sure the value is less than 1 (like 0.7 or 0.5).
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added an opacity property to the .box1 CSS rule with a value between 0 and 1 (exclusive).
